compare_blocks.title: The key difference

compare_blocks.body:
The table fixes one film, one batch of material, one script and one release window. If one is the lead editor and the other only helping out, or the material runs to twenty clips instead of two hundred, those conditions cover both columns.

Each row records the ground likely to be attended to, and the last column names the axis it leans to. Either type can use either approach; the rows record only which ground is taken first, and the shared S means the grounds in both columns ultimately have to be checkable against the material and the cut.

| The same task (same film, same material, same window) | ESFP: ground likely to be attended to | ISTJ: ground likely to be attended to | What this row turns on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In a short-video team these two get filed as the same practical sort: neither enjoys a vague ideas meeting, both say show me something, and both ask how exactly we shoot this while other people are discussing tone.

That agreement comes from the shared S: both want checkable material, a finished cut and things that actually happened, and neither buys a plan that exists only as a concept. But S only says the entrance is the same; E/I, T/F and J/P all differ, so practical is only the shared shell. The difference is where that practicality points: one more often at the people and reactions on set, the other more often at accumulated records and standards.

The three preferences have to be read separately. E/I asks whether attention and energy land on the scene outside or go back into inner sorting first; T/F asks whether judgement takes a person's situation and values first or a standard that can be checked consistently; J/P asks whether an arrangement is fixed outward first or options are kept. None substitutes for another, and none can be read from speed, the order of actions or a change of mind on the day.

### ESFP and ISTJ: the three-second opening, test it or calculate it

Same task: the script says only that the opening has to grab people. Both routes for taking evidence are reasonable, but they prove different things.

The on-set route usually runs like this: set up and shoot three versions — a hands-on demonstration, a counter-intuitive line, a cut straight into a failure — watch the playback, and pick the one you yourself want to keep watching. It gives a watchable sample under this batch of material and this kind of delivery; it is fast and often catches something the script missed. Its cost is a sample of one, which makes it easy to take your own judgement for the audience's.

The historical-data route usually runs like this: pull the first three seconds of retention for the past twenty films, count which type of opening loses people fastest, and write a version from the conclusion. It gives a pattern for this account's audience over that period; it is steady. Its cost is that audience, subject and placement may all have changed, so applying an old conclusion to a new subject can also repeat a device until the audience is tired of it.

The two routes are not one thing at two speeds; they are two kinds of evidence — one answers how this looks now, the other answers how this category performed before. A workable combination is to draw the no-go area first, listing the opening types already known to lose people, then shoot three versions inside that space and compare them over the same window; the verification conditions are set out below.

There is no starting-point criterion here. An ESFP who has made dozens of films will also look at the retention curve, and an ISTJ working a familiar subject may start shooting on experience; that belongs to experience and task conditions, changes no preference, and cannot be used to define anyone.

### ESFP and ISTJ: sharing Te and Fi with the seats swapped

In the common four-position writing used here, ESFP is Se–Fi–Te–Ni and ISTJ is Si–Te–Fi–Ne. Two of the four names coincide, Te and Fi; the other two are the same family in a different attitude, Se against Si and Ni against Ne. ESFP puts Fi second and Te third; ISTJ puts Te second and Fi third.

The swap describes theoretical emphasis, not a production sequence. ESFP's judging more often lands first on whether this feels right and rings true, then uses Te to schedule the execution; ISTJ's more often raises the standard, the delivery and the deadline first, with Fi behind. Reading the same script, the two may therefore draw different emphases: one asks whether the film feels like the real thing, the other asks what is being delivered, by when and to what specification.

But position does not dictate who starts or who finishes, and does not explain why someone produced a particular cut. Whether the third position is marked introverted or extraverted is not agreed between tables: this page uses one common writing that marks the third process, while other sources may give only the function name. That disagreement affects neither of the first two positions and does not explain the timing of actions. Base descriptions sit at the [ESFP profile](/en/personality/esfp) and the [ISTJ profile](/en/personality/istj).

compare_blocks.body:
The fictional examples use shared conditions to compare what people might weigh in a decision. Assign real work based on experience, willingness and the task’s needs. Either person could use either approach.

### ESFP and ISTJ: the three-second opening of a short film

(Fictional scene) The previous section compared what each kind of evidence can prove; this one looks at a specific film.

A short film about a vacuum flask sells twelve hours of heat retention. One opening lifts the flask out of ice water and pours a cup of steaming tea. The other is white text on black: measured over twelve hours, water fell from 98 to 71 degrees.

The first makes people want to watch to the end; the second makes them believe it. Both have a blind spot: a gripping image that never states the selling point leaves viewers unsure what is for sale, and clear data that opens like a manual gets swiped away within three seconds.

To see which suits this placement, treat it as a hypothesis to test rather than a conclusion. Where conditions allow, split traffic randomly in the same window, holding audience, budget, placement and everything after the opening constant, and look only at three-second retention and product-page clicks, stating whether the denominator is impressions or plays. High retention with low clicks only suggests the hook and the selling point may have come apart; high clicks with low retention only suggests the opening may not have caught people — either needs another round before a judgement.

Where conditions cannot be controlled and the versions go out on different days, audience and time slot may differ, so a change in the metric cannot be attributed to the opening and is only an early clue; nor is finished-cut data used to verify a type, since the two have no correspondence.

### ESFP and ISTJ: filming an oral history with a grandmother

(Fictional scene) The family wants a video of a grandmother who is eighty. One approach sets up the camera and talks with her, following whatever she raises, and may catch the moment she talks about crying quietly when she was young. The other writes a question list first: which year she was born, which year she entered the factory, how many people in the household, whether there are old photographs to copy.

The first catches feeling but some dates and places do not line up; the second is complete but may make her feel she is being interviewed. This is not about who is more dutiful; each way of recording is missing half.

A workable method is two sittings: first the facts from the list, then a session with no list at all, just talking with her; cut them interleaved, with the list holding the facts up and the conversation supplying the feeling. Before rolling, ask whether she is willing to be filmed and which things she does not want to discuss — that question outranks any list.

### ESFP and ISTJ: the client wants sixty seconds cut to fifteen

(Fictional scene) The client announces that the placement only takes fifteen seconds. One approach reviews the material for the three most striking images and cuts a fast new version. The other confirms which few pieces of information must survive those fifteen seconds, then cuts by priority.

A visually striking edit can lose key information, while an edit that keeps every required detail can be hard to follow. Agree on the must-keep information and let the person with the relevant experience decide how best to show it. One person can do both jobs.

### ESFP and ISTJ: planning dinner with friends

In this fictional example, two friends are arranging dinner for the same six guests. They have the same messages, budget and dietary requirements. Two restaurants meet those requirements, and either friend can make the booking by Friday.

One consideration is the value of confirming a restaurant now so everyone can plan. Another is the value of keeping both options open until the group replies, with Friday as the booking cutoff. This illustrates the J/P distinction between settling an outward arrangement and keeping options open. Either friend could weigh both considerations or make the booking. The timing of the booking tells you nothing conclusive about their type.
compare_blocks.title: The difference in a real scene

compare_blocks.body:
Who is better at filming cannot serve as evidence. Feel comes from a great deal of shooting, and judgement from long record-keeping and review; both are trained capacities, not something a preference supplies.

Who is more rigid is a misread too. An ISTJ improvises on a familiar subject, and an ESFP writes a shot list on an important project. Treating rule-keeping as a lack of ideas, and casualness as unprofessional, bends the reading.

The third misread uses tidiness as evidence of J or P. Whether a desktop is messy or files are named has very little to do with preference, and a great deal to do with work habits, team norms and the pace of the current project.

The fourth takes the first move as evidence. Opening the camera or opening the analytics dashboard depends on role, the amount of material, the deadline and the last film's result; the same person making opposite choices on two films is common.

The fifth reads S as only seeing what is in front of you. Either type can discuss positioning and a six-month content plan; what they more often ask during that discussion is that it come back down to specific material, cases and checkable conditions.

### ESFP and ISTJ: the three-second opening of a short film
(Fictional scene) The previous section compared what each kind of evidence can prove; this one looks at a specific film.

A short film about a vacuum flask sells twelve hours of heat retention. One opening lifts the flask out of ice water and pours a cup of steaming tea. The other is white text on black: measured over twelve hours, water fell from 98 to 71 degrees.

The first makes people want to watch to the end; the second makes them believe it. Both have a blind spot: a gripping image that never states the selling point leaves viewers unsure what is for sale, and clear data that opens like a manual gets swiped away within three seconds.

To see which suits this placement, treat it as a hypothesis to test rather than a conclusion. Where conditions allow, split traffic randomly in the same window, holding audience, budget, placement and everything after the opening constant, and look only at three-second retention and product-page clicks, stating whether the denominator is impressions or plays. sections.title: Quick answer

body: In a short-video team these two get filed as the same practical sort: neither enjoys a vague ideas meeting, both say show me something, and both ask how exactly we shoot this while other people are discussing tone.

That agreement comes from the shared S: both want checkable material, a finished cut and things that actually happened, and neither buys a plan that exists only as a concept. But S only says the entrance is the same; E/I, T/F and J/P all differ, so practical is only the shared shell. The difference is where that practicality points: one more often at the people and reactions on set, the other more often at accumulated records and standards.

The three preferences have to be read separately. E/I asks whether attention and energy land on the scene outside or go back into inner sorting first; T/F asks whether judgement takes a person's situation and values first or a standard that can be checked consistently; J/P asks whether an arrangement is fixed outward first or options are kept. None substitutes for another, and none can be read from speed, the order of actions or a change of mind on the day.
### ESFP and ISTJ: the three-second opening, test it or calculate it
Same task: the script says only that the opening has to grab people. Both routes for taking evidence are reasonable, but they prove different things.

The on-set route usually runs like this: set up and shoot three versions — a hands-on demonstration, a counter-intuitive line, a cut straight into a failure — watch the playback, and pick the one you yourself want to keep watching. It gives a watchable sample under this batch of material and this kind of delivery; it is fast and often catches something the script missed. Its cost is a sample of one, which makes it easy to take your own judgement for the audience's.

The historical-data route usually runs like this: pull the first three seconds of retention for the past twenty films, count which type of opening loses people fastest, and write a version from the conclusion. It gives a pattern for this account's audience over that period; it is steady. Its cost is that audience, subject and placement may all have changed, so applying an old conclusion to a new subject can also repeat a device until the audience is tired of it.

The two routes are not one thing at two speeds; they are two kinds of evidence — one answers how this looks now, the other answers how this category performed before. A workable combination is to draw the no-go area first, listing the opening types already known to lose people, then shoot three versions inside that space and compare them over the same window; the verification conditions are set out below.

There is no starting-point criterion here. An ESFP who has made dozens of films will also look at the retention curve, and an ISTJ working a familiar subject may start shooting on experience; that belongs to experience and task conditions, changes no preference, and cannot be used to define anyone.
### ESFP and ISTJ: sharing Te and Fi with the seats swapped

In the common four-position writing used here, ESFP is Se–Fi–Te–Ni and ISTJ is Si–Te–Fi–Ne. Two of the four names coincide, Te and Fi; the other two are the same family in a different attitude, Se against Si and Ni against Ne. ESFP puts Fi second and Te third; ISTJ puts Te second and Fi third.

The swap describes theoretical emphasis, not a production sequence. ESFP's judging more often lands first on whether this feels right and rings true, then uses Te to schedule the execution; ISTJ's more often raises the standard, the delivery and the deadline first, with Fi behind. Reading the same script, the two may therefore draw different emphases: one asks whether the film feels like the real thing, the other asks what is being delivered, by when and to what specification.

But position does not dictate who starts or who finishes, and does not explain why someone produced a particular cut. Whether the third position is marked introverted or extraverted is not agreed between tables: this page uses one common writing that marks the third process, while other sources may give only the function name. That disagreement affects neither of the first two positions and does not explain the timing of actions. Base descriptions sit at the [ESFP profile](/en/personality/esfp) and the [ISTJ profile](/en/personality/istj).

body: The table fixes one film, one batch of material, one script and one release window. If one is the lead editor and the other only helping out, or the material runs to twenty clips instead of two hundred, those conditions cover both columns.

Each row records the ground likely to be attended to, and the last column names the axis it leans to. Either type can use either approach; the rows record only which ground is taken first, and the shared S means the grounds in both columns ultimately have to be checkable against the material and the cut.

| The same task (same film, same material, same window) | ESFP: ground likely to be attended to | ISTJ: ground likely to be attended to | What this row turns on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Asked in the ideas meeting how the opening should go | Talk it through while gesturing, letting the room's reaction set the direction | Run it through privately, then give a formed answer | Direction of attention, leaning E/I |
| Reviewing this film after the shoot | Talk it over with someone and work out what was right in the telling | Go back over the day's notes and data alone | Where energy goes, leaning E/I |
| The client changes the brief late | Ask what feeling you want, and what this change means for the people watching | Confirm the delivery date, the specification and the information that must survive | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F |
| Numbers are flat after release, where to look first | Weigh which of the same documented issues most affects the intended audience | Apply the same performance criteria to the same metrics and feasible changes | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F |
| Two hundred clips in the bin | Keep more than one workable editing order open while reviewing the same clips | Agree on a provisional editing order for the same clips, with room to revise it | Arrangement outward, leaning J/P |
| Thirty films in a row | Sustain the effort through what changes on set and what is new | Sustain output through a fixed process and a checklist | Arrangement outward, leaning J/P |

No row is a competence scale. An ESFP with years of commercial work checks the client's and the platform's hard requirements first, and an ISTJ new to the job may shoot a few to find the feel. One person changes approach with the amount of material, the deadline, the last result and who is waiting for the cut, so these rows cannot be used to classify anyone.

body: The fictional examples use shared conditions to compare what people might weigh in a decision. Assign real work based on experience, willingness and the task’s needs. Either person could use either approach.
### ESFP and ISTJ: the three-second opening of a short film
(Fictional scene) The previous section compared what each kind of evidence can prove; this one looks at a specific film.

A short film about a vacuum flask sells twelve hours of heat retention. One opening lifts the flask out of ice water and pours a cup of steaming tea. The other is white text on black: measured over twelve hours, water fell from 98 to 71 degrees.

The first makes people want to watch to the end; the second makes them believe it. Both have a blind spot: a gripping image that never states the selling point leaves viewers unsure what is for sale, and clear data that opens like a manual gets swiped away within three seconds.

To see which suits this placement, treat it as a hypothesis to test rather than a conclusion. Where conditions allow, split traffic randomly in the same window, holding audience, budget, placement and everything after the opening constant, and look only at three-second retention and product-page clicks, stating whether the denominator is impressions or plays. High retention with low clicks only suggests the hook and the selling point may have come apart; high clicks with low retention only suggests the opening may not have caught people — either needs another round before a judgement.

Where conditions cannot be controlled and the versions go out on different days, audience and time slot may differ, so a change in the metric cannot be attributed to the opening and is only an early clue; nor is finished-cut data used to verify a type, since the two have no correspondence.
### ESFP and ISTJ: filming an oral history with a grandmother

(Fictional scene) The family wants a video of a grandmother who is eighty. One approach sets up the camera and talks with her, following whatever she raises, and may catch the moment she talks about crying quietly when she was young. The other writes a question list first: which year she was born, which year she entered the factory, how many people in the household, whether there are old photographs to copy.

The first catches feeling but some dates and places do not line up; the second is complete but may make her feel she is being interviewed. This is not about who is more dutiful; each way of recording is missing half.

A workable method is two sittings: first the facts from the list, then a session with no list at all, just talking with her; cut them interleaved, with the list holding the facts up and the conversation supplying the feeling. Before rolling, ask whether she is willing to be filmed and which things she does not want to discuss — that question outranks any list.
### ESFP and ISTJ: the client wants sixty seconds cut to fifteen

(Fictional scene) The client announces that the placement only takes fifteen seconds. One approach reviews the material for the three most striking images and cuts a fast new version. The other confirms which few pieces of information must survive those fifteen seconds, then cuts by priority.

A visually striking edit can lose key information, while an edit that keeps every required detail can be hard to follow. Agree on the must-keep information and let the person with the relevant experience decide how best to show it. One person can do both jobs.

### ESFP and ISTJ: planning dinner with friends

In this fictional example, two friends are arranging dinner for the same six guests. They have the same messages, budget and dietary requirements. Two restaurants meet those requirements, and either friend can make the booking by Friday.

One consideration is the value of confirming a restaurant now so everyone can plan. Another is the value of keeping both options open until the group replies, with Friday as the booking cutoff. This illustrates the J/P distinction between settling an outward arrangement and keeping options open. Either friend could weigh both considerations or make the booking. The timing of the booking tells you nothing conclusive about their type.

body: Who is better at filming cannot serve as evidence. Feel comes from a great deal of shooting, and judgement from long record-keeping and review; both are trained capacities, not something a preference supplies.

Who is more rigid is a misread too. An ISTJ improvises on a familiar subject, and an ESFP writes a shot list on an important project. Treating rule-keeping as a lack of ideas, and casualness as unprofessional, bends the reading.

The third misread uses tidiness as evidence of J or P. Whether a desktop is messy or files are named has very little to do with preference, and a great deal to do with work habits, team norms and the pace of the current project.

The fourth takes the first move as evidence. Opening the camera or opening the analytics dashboard depends on role, the amount of material, the deadline and the last film's result; the same person making opposite choices on two films is common.

The fifth reads S as only seeing what is in front of you. Either type can discuss positioning and a six-month content plan; what they more often ask during that discussion is that it come back down to specific material, cases and checkable conditions.

body: When two results differ, check the item bank, version, language and scoring notes first, then the work you were doing when you answered: had you just taken on a project that needed improvisation, or just been asked to deliver to a specification? A situation pushes answers to one side, and one score cannot establish a stable tendency.

The exercise can be designed like this: take a few recent films and write a few lines on each — what information I had at the start, what constraints the task set (deadline, budget, client requirements), which route I took and why; a few days after release add one line on whether the result overturned that judgement. What gets recorded is the conditions and the trade-off, to understand why the strategy changed; no type labels on the notes, and no accuracy rate calculated.
If the two routes alternate, you have built your own mixed practice while accumulating experience, which is normal.

body: **Framework sources**: the definitions of the four preferences follow the [Myers-Briggs official facts page](https://www.myersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts); the type-dynamics framework follows the [Foundation's note on type dynamics](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) and the [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/).

**Four-position convention on this page**: Se–Fi–Te–Ni for ESFP and Si–Te–Fi–Ne for ISTJ follow the common in-site writing, and the attitude of the third process is marked differently between sources; this page takes one of them as an editorial convention and does not present it as the Foundation's only reading.

**Editorial fiction note**: the opening, the vacuum flask, the oral history, the recut and the dinner plan are fictional, used only to practise telling grounds apart, and correspond to no real person, brand or organisation.

**Research scope**: [McCrae and Costa (1989)](https://scholars.duke.edu/publication/1458465) found no support for treating the preferences measured by the 1985 MBTI as strictly divided categories and found overlap with several dimensions of the five-factor model. [Erford et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcad.70006) reviewed studies of the English MBTI Form M. That review concerns evidence about one instrument; it does not test the fictional scenarios here or establish how an ESFP or ISTJ will act in a specific situation.

**Scope limits**: the remarks on retention, clicks and traffic splitting are method examples and do not constitute a statistical conclusion about any account's performance; a result has to be read against the item bank and the situation it was answered from, and is not for ranking ability, hiring screens or predicting relationships. The scoring and evidence scope of the FermatMind assessment is set out in the [assessment method notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).

sections.body_md:
ESFP and ISTJ are two of the sixteen types, sharing only S and differing on E/I, T/F and J/P. Each of the three has its own meaning, and they cannot be compressed into one being casual and the other rigid.

- **S (shared)**: when taking in information both more often start from checkable fact, concrete experience and what has already happened, rather than from concept and hypothesis. It describes the entrance for material, not only seeing what is in front of you — an ESFP chasing detail on set and an ISTJ pulling old records both sit inside it.
- **E/I**: ESFP's E turns attention and energy more often to other people, events and the scene unfolding; ISTJ's I turns more often back to inner sorting and existing experience. It describes direction, not social skill and not how much anyone talks.
- **T/F**: ESFP's F more often puts people, relationships and values into judgement; ISTJ's T more often judges on an objective standard that can be checked consistently.
- **J/P**: ISTJ's J more often forms an arrangement and a conclusion outward first; ESFP's P more often keeps options and adjusts to new information as the work goes.

The stacks follow the common four-position writing used here: Se–Fi–Te–Ni for ESFP and Si–Te–Fi–Ne for ISTJ. Two names are shared, Te and Fi, with the seats swapped; Se against Si and Ne against Ni are the same family in a different attitude. The attitude of the third process is marked differently elsewhere, and this arrangement is an editorial convention, not the Foundation's only reading.

One boundary: on the same film, shooting a test first or checking the data first are two strategies for one task, and either type may use either; that shows how evidence was taken this time, not which type the person is.
sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
In a short-video team these two get filed as the same practical sort: neither enjoys a vague ideas meeting, both say show me something, and both ask how exactly we shoot this while other people are discussing tone.

That agreement comes from the shared S: both want checkable material, a finished cut and things that actually happened, and neither buys a plan that exists only as a concept. But S only says the entrance is the same; E/I, T/F and J/P all differ, so practical is only the shared shell. The difference is where that practicality points: one more often at the people and reactions on set, the other more often at accumulated records and standards.

The three preferences have to be read separately. E/I asks whether attention and energy land on the scene outside or go back into inner sorting first; T/F asks whether judgement takes a person's situation and values first or a standard that can be checked consistently; J/P asks whether an arrangement is fixed outward first or options are kept. None substitutes for another, and none can be read from speed, the order of actions or a change of mind on the day.

### ESFP and ISTJ: the three-second opening, test it or calculate it

Same task: the script says only that the opening has to grab people. Both routes for taking evidence are reasonable, but they prove different things.

The on-set route usually runs like this: set up and shoot three versions — a hands-on demonstration, a counter-intuitive line, a cut straight into a failure — watch the playback, and pick the one you yourself want to keep watching. It gives a watchable sample under this batch of material and this kind of delivery; it is fast and often catches something the script missed. Its cost is a sample of one, which makes it easy to take your own judgement for the audience's.

The historical-data route usually runs like this: pull the first three seconds of retention for the past twenty films, count which type of opening loses people fastest, and write a version from the conclusion. It gives a pattern for this account's audience over that period; it is steady. Its cost is that audience, subject and placement may all have changed, so applying an old conclusion to a new subject can also repeat a device until the audience is tired of it.

The two routes are not one thing at two speeds; they are two kinds of evidence — one answers how this looks now, the other answers how this category performed before. A workable combination is to draw the no-go area first, listing the opening types already known to lose people, then shoot three versions inside that space and compare them over the same window; the verification conditions are set out below.

There is no starting-point criterion here. An ESFP who has made dozens of films will also look at the retention curve, and an ISTJ working a familiar subject may start shooting on experience; that belongs to experience and task conditions, changes no preference, and cannot be used to define anyone.

### ESFP and ISTJ: sharing Te and Fi with the seats swapped

In the common four-position writing used here, ESFP is Se–Fi–Te–Ni and ISTJ is Si–Te–Fi–Ne. Two of the four names coincide, Te and Fi; the other two are the same family in a different attitude, Se against Si and Ni against Ne. ESFP puts Fi second and Te third; ISTJ puts Te second and Fi third.

The swap describes theoretical emphasis, not a production sequence. ESFP's judging more often lands first on whether this feels right and rings true, then uses Te to schedule the execution; ISTJ's more often raises the standard, the delivery and the deadline first, with Fi behind. Reading the same script, the two may therefore draw different emphases: one asks whether the film feels like the real thing, the other asks what is being delivered, by when and to what specification.

But position does not dictate who starts or who finishes, and does not explain why someone produced a particular cut. Whether the third position is marked introverted or extraverted is not agreed between tables: this page uses one common writing that marks the third process, while other sources may give only the function name. That disagreement affects neither of the first two positions and does not explain the timing of actions. Base descriptions sit at the [ESFP profile](/en/personality/esfp) and the [ISTJ profile](/en/personality/istj).

sections.body_md:
The table fixes one film, one batch of material, one script and one release window. If one is the lead editor and the other only helping out, or the material runs to twenty clips instead of two hundred, those conditions cover both columns.

Each row records the ground likely to be attended to, and the last column names the axis it leans to. Either type can use either approach; the rows record only which ground is taken first, and the shared S means the grounds in both columns ultimately have to be checkable against the material and the cut.

| The same task (same film, same material, same window) | ESFP: ground likely to be attended to | ISTJ: ground likely to be attended to | What this row turns on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Asked in the ideas meeting how the opening should go | Talk it through while gesturing, letting the room's reaction set the direction | Run it through privately, then give a formed answer | Direction of attention, leaning E/I |
| Reviewing this film after the shoot | Talk it over with someone and work out what was right in the telling | Go back over the day's notes and data alone | Where energy goes, leaning E/I |
| The client changes the brief late | Ask what feeling you want, and what this change means for the people watching | Confirm the delivery date, the specification and the information that must survive | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F |
| Numbers are flat after release, where to look first | Weigh which of the same documented issues most affects the intended audience | Apply the same performance criteria to the same metrics and feasible changes | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F |
| Two hundred clips in the bin | Keep more than one workable editing order open while reviewing the same clips | Agree on a provisional editing order for the same clips, with room to revise it | Arrangement outward, leaning J/P |
| Thirty films in a row | Sustain the effort through what changes on set and what is new | Sustain output through a fixed process and a checklist | Arrangement outward, leaning J/P |

No row is a competence scale. An ESFP with years of commercial work checks the client's and the platform's hard requirements first, and an ISTJ new to the job may shoot a few to find the feel. One person changes approach with the amount of material, the deadline, the last result and who is waiting for the cut, so these rows cannot be used to classify anyone.
sections.title: ESFP and ISTJ in one minute

sections.body_md:
The fictional examples use shared conditions to compare what people might weigh in a decision. Assign real work based on experience, willingness and the task’s needs. Either person could use either approach.

### ESFP and ISTJ: the three-second opening of a short film

(Fictional scene) The previous section compared what each kind of evidence can prove; this one looks at a specific film.

A short film about a vacuum flask sells twelve hours of heat retention. One opening lifts the flask out of ice water and pours a cup of steaming tea. The other is white text on black: measured over twelve hours, water fell from 98 to 71 degrees.

The first makes people want to watch to the end; the second makes them believe it. Both have a blind spot: a gripping image that never states the selling point leaves viewers unsure what is for sale, and clear data that opens like a manual gets swiped away within three seconds.

To see which suits this placement, treat it as a hypothesis to test rather than a conclusion. Where conditions allow, split traffic randomly in the same window, holding audience, budget, placement and everything after the opening constant, and look only at three-second retention and product-page clicks, stating whether the denominator is impressions or plays. High retention with low clicks only suggests the hook and the selling point may have come apart; high clicks with low retention only suggests the opening may not have caught people — either needs another round before a judgement.

Where conditions cannot be controlled and the versions go out on different days, audience and time slot may differ, so a change in the metric cannot be attributed to the opening and is only an early clue; nor is finished-cut data used to verify a type, since the two have no correspondence.

### ESFP and ISTJ: filming an oral history with a grandmother

(Fictional scene) The family wants a video of a grandmother who is eighty. One approach sets up the camera and talks with her, following whatever she raises, and may catch the moment she talks about crying quietly when she was young. The other writes a question list first: which year she was born, which year she entered the factory, how many people in the household, whether there are old photographs to copy.

The first catches feeling but some dates and places do not line up; the second is complete but may make her feel she is being interviewed. This is not about who is more dutiful; each way of recording is missing half.

A workable method is two sittings: first the facts from the list, then a session with no list at all, just talking with her; cut them interleaved, with the list holding the facts up and the conversation supplying the feeling. Before rolling, ask whether she is willing to be filmed and which things she does not want to discuss — that question outranks any list.

### ESFP and ISTJ: the client wants sixty seconds cut to fifteen

(Fictional scene) The client announces that the placement only takes fifteen seconds. One approach reviews the material for the three most striking images and cuts a fast new version. The other confirms which few pieces of information must survive those fifteen seconds, then cuts by priority.

A visually striking edit can lose key information, while an edit that keeps every required detail can be hard to follow. Agree on the must-keep information and let the person with the relevant experience decide how best to show it. One person can do both jobs.

### ESFP and ISTJ: planning dinner with friends

In this fictional example, two friends are arranging dinner for the same six guests. They have the same messages, budget and dietary requirements. Two restaurants meet those requirements, and either friend can make the booking by Friday.

One consideration is the value of confirming a restaurant now so everyone can plan. Another is the value of keeping both options open until the group replies, with Friday as the booking cutoff. This illustrates the J/P distinction between settling an outward arrangement and keeping options open. Either friend could weigh both considerations or make the booking. The timing of the booking tells you nothing conclusive about their type.
sections.title: ESFP and ISTJ at work and with friends

sections.body_md:
Who is better at filming cannot serve as evidence. Feel comes from a great deal of shooting, and judgement from long record-keeping and review; both are trained capacities, not something a preference supplies.

Who is more rigid is a misread too. An ISTJ improvises on a familiar subject, and an ESFP writes a shot list on an important project. Treating rule-keeping as a lack of ideas, and casualness as unprofessional, bends the reading.

The third misread uses tidiness as evidence of J or P. Whether a desktop is messy or files are named has very little to do with preference, and a great deal to do with work habits, team norms and the pace of the current project.

The fourth takes the first move as evidence. Opening the camera or opening the analytics dashboard depends on role, the amount of material, the deadline and the last film's result; the same person making opposite choices on two films is common.

The fifth reads S as only seeing what is in front of you. Either type can discuss positioning and a six-month content plan; what they more often ask during that discussion is that it come back down to specific material, cases and checkable conditions.
sections.title: ESFP and ISTJ: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When two results differ, check the item bank, version, language and scoring notes first, then the work you were doing when you answered: had you just taken on a project that needed improvisation, or just been asked to deliver to a specification? A situation pushes answers to one side, and one score cannot establish a stable tendency.

The exercise can be designed like this: take a few recent films and write a few lines on each — what information I had at the start, what constraints the task set (deadline, budget, client requirements), which route I took and why; a few days after release add one line on whether the result overturned that judgement. What gets recorded is the conditions and the trade-off, to understand why the strategy changed; no type labels on the notes, and no accuracy rate calculated.

If the two routes alternate, you have built your own mixed practice while accumulating experience, which is normal.
sections.title: ESFP and ISTJ: how to keep observing

items.answer:
Because the seats are swapped: ESFP has Fi second and Te third, ISTJ has Te second and Fi third, so the theoretical emphasis differs — one checks whether the segment feels right, the other raises the standard and the deadline first.

But that explains only which ground is taken first, not how a particular film opens. With the same script, either may go to the data first and either may shoot a version first, depending on whether there is enough material, how tight the deadline is and how the last similar film performed.
items.question: They share Te and Fi — why do their openings so often differ?

items.answer:
Often not the same layer. One more often asks why this film made people stop, using playback, comments and the feel in the room; the other more often asks how this type of opening performed across the last twenty films.

The two complement each other: the first finds new variables, the second confirms a stable pattern; the first alone chases lucky hits, the second alone misses that the audience has already changed. That is a matter of experience and method, and either type can lean either way.
items.question: Both care about data — is it the same data?

items.answer:
They are not exceptions. Preference describes which ground is taken first, not a checklist of behaviour; with practice the other side's approach also becomes available.

What is worth watching is the reason: on the same film, did you want a watchable sample first or a checkable standard first? A reason that recurs across several comparable situations says more about the entrance than a single style does. If both feel natural, you have trained both approaches.
items.question: ISTJ also shoots lively material, ESFP also works to a script — are those exceptions?

items.answer:
Not by type. The first three seconds, information density, transition rhythm and the closing call to action can all be done by either, and who takes which follows experience, willingness and the manpower of the moment.

A workable method is to have both cut the same material, then ask a few people who have not seen it to say what the film is selling; the version that gets retold most accurately usually used both kinds of consideration. That is a small-sample exploratory check, not proof of effect, and certainly not a way to verify a type.
items.question: A fifteen-second film — which three seconds does each own?

items.answer:
Most easily between this is enough and this has not been checked: one feels the emotion has arrived and it can go out, the other feels the information is not aligned and it cannot.

A workable agreement sets a lock time for each film: it must go out at that point, and the stretch before it is reserved for checking only, with no further creative changes. This conflict comes from current responsibility and risk-bearing, not from type; on another project or with another client the two may swap sides.
items.question: Editing together, where do ESFP and ISTJ most easily jam?

items.answer:
Check the item bank itself first: whether the instrument's name, version, language and scoring are consistent, and whether you were answering from a work project or from home.

If more observation is wanted, go back over the work records you left — not to infer a type from whether folders are named, but to see what information you had, what constrained you and why that route was chosen. These are corroboration only, not conclusions; what matters remains which ground is taken first across several comparable situations.

**Framework sources**: the definitions of the four preferences follow the [Myers-Briggs official facts page](https://www.myersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts); the type-dynamics framework follows the [Foundation's note on type dynamics](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) and the [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/).

**Four-position convention on this page**: Se–Fi–Te–Ni for ESFP and Si–Te–Fi–Ne for ISTJ follow the common in-site writing, and the attitude of the third process is marked differently between sources; this page takes one of them as an editorial convention and does not present it as the Foundation's only reading.

**Editorial fiction note**: the opening, the vacuum flask, the oral history, the recut and the dinner plan are fictional, used only to practise telling grounds apart, and correspond to no real person, brand or organisation.

**Research scope**: [McCrae and Costa (1989)](https://scholars.duke.edu/publication/1458465) found no support for treating the preferences measured by the 1985 MBTI as strictly divided categories and found overlap with several dimensions of the five-factor model. [Erford et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcad.70006) reviewed studies of the English MBTI Form M. That review concerns evidence about one instrument; it does not test the fictional scenarios here or establish how an ESFP or ISTJ will act in a specific situation.

**Scope limits**: the remarks on retention, clicks and traffic splitting are method examples and do not constitute a statistical conclusion about any account's performance; a result has to be read against the item bank and the situation it was answered from, and is not for ranking ability, hiring screens or predicting relationships. The scoring and evidence scope of the FermatMind assessment is set out in the [assessment method notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).
